q.intro.text: A bike shop charges a one-time fee plus a price per hour. The table shows three rentals. Two hours cost thirty-four dollars, four hours cost fifty dollars, and six hours cost sixty-six dollars. How big is the fee: the cost before you ride at all? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the graph moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: From two to four hours, the cost goes from thirty-four to fifty dollars: sixteen dollars more for two hours. Per one hour, sixteen divided by two is eight. The rate is eight dollars per hour.

e.step1.text: Now walk back from two hours to zero hours. Two hours less takes away two times eight, sixteen dollars. Thirty-four minus sixteen is eighteen. At zero hours the cost is eighteen dollars. That is the fee: b is eighteen.

e.step2.text: The cost is eight dollars for every hour, plus the eighteen dollar fee. C equals eight h plus eighteen, where C is the cost in dollars and h is the time in hours.

e.step3.text: Check it on a row we did not use: eight times six plus eighteen is sixty-six. It fits every row, so C equals eight h plus eighteen is the rule.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is the fee eighteen dollars, and not thirty-four?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Thirty-four dollars already includes two hours of riding. The fee is the cost at zero hours.

e.why.first.text: The first row is two hours, not zero hours. Thirty-four dollars is the fee plus two hours of riding.

e.why.swap.text: The price per hour is the rate, eight dollars. The fee is paid once, at the start.

t.intro.text: A phone battery runs down at a steady rate. At five minutes it shows eighty-five percent, at fifteen minutes sixty-five percent, and at twenty-five minutes forty-five percent. The rate is done for you.

t.rate.text: Every ten minutes the battery loses twenty points. Per one minute that is minus two: two points down each minute.

t.b.text: Your step: what did the battery show at zero minutes? Type b.

t.b.ok.text: Yes. Going back five minutes adds back five times two, ten points. Eighty-five plus ten is ninety-five. b is ninety-five.

t.b.first.text: Eighty-five percent is the reading at five minutes. Go back five more minutes, to zero.

t.b.sign.text: Going back in time, the battery was fuller. Add the ten points, don’t take them away.

t.b.no.text: Start at eighty-five percent at five minutes. Each minute back adds two points.

t.eq.text: Your step: which equation fits? B is the battery in percent, and t is the time in minutes.

t.eq.ok.text: Yes. Start at ninety-five, down two each minute. B equals minus two t plus ninety-five.

t.eq.swap.text: That multiplies the start by t. The rate, minus two, multiplies t. The start, ninety-five, stands alone.

t.eq.sign.text: The battery goes down, so the rate is negative: minus two, not plus two.

t.check.text: Check it: what does your equation give at t equals twenty-five?

t.check.ok.text: Minus two times twenty-five, plus ninety-five, is forty-five: the same as the table. The equation fits.

t.check.sign.text: Mind the sign. Minus two times twenty-five is minus fifty. Minus fifty plus ninety-five is what?

t.check.no.text: Minus two times twenty-five is minus fifty. Then add ninety-five.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked eighteen dollars, and you were right. Now you can show why: walk back to zero hours with the rate.

q.cb.first.text: At the start you picked thirty-four dollars. That is the cost of two hours. The fee is the cost at zero hours.

q.cb.zero.text: At the start you picked zero dollars. But there is a fee, so the line starts at eighteen dollars, not at zero.

q.cb.none.text: Rate first, per one unit. Then walk back to input zero for b.

p.intro.text: Jordan says: two hours cost thirty-four dollars, so four hours cost sixty-eight. Twice the time, twice the cost. Is Jordan right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The table says four hours cost fifty dollars. Jordan’s sixty-eight is off the line.

p.c2.text: Right. Only the eight h part doubles. The eighteen dollar fee is paid once, so doubling counts it twice.

p.c3.text: Right. A proportional line goes through zero, zero. This one starts at eighteen.

p.no.prop.text: Straight means linear, not proportional. A proportional line must also go through zero, zero.

p.no.scale.text: Going up every hour is not enough. The fee does not grow with the hours, so the cost does not double.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the graph backs every one. The rental is linear, but not proportional.
